title: Beyond Either-Or: A Platonic Dialectical Resolution of Recognition Conflicts in Academic Promotion at African Universities
authors: Eutychus Ngotho Gichuru; Archangel Byaruhanga Rukooko
institutions: Makerere University
abstract: The research uses Platonic dialectical analysis to study the positive views African academic staff members who did not receive promotions have about Ubuntu-based evaluative standards while the promoted faculty members show negative views about these standards. The researchers analyze this paradox through systematic literature review and theoretical synthesis which uses dialectical methods to examine opposing viewpoints until reaching higher understanding. The analysis shows that both parties involved two groups who raised genuine issues but their viewpoints contained mutual contradictions. The rejected academics identified the epistemological violence present in bibliometric systems but they tended to romanticize Ubuntu as a flaw-free solution while the promoted academics established their case for transparency through their defence of transparent standards. The material conditions of knowledge production institutional double consciousness and the political economy of African higher education create two different ways people view academic research. The process of authentic synthesis needs multiple evaluation systems which acknowledge different types of academic excellence and material conditions which allow such excellence to exist and the need to rebuild scholarly communities which audit culture has scattered into separate parts. The study presents educational development scholarship with dialectical methodology proof which shows how educational development conflicts create conflicting institutional conflicts which lead to synthetic institutional innovations.

title: Enhancing author rankings with a comprehensive research profile index
authors: Ilyas Ahmad; Abdul Shahid; Sana Ullah Khan; Khan Bahadar Khan; Yiming Deng
institutions: Kohat University of Science and Technology; Michigan State University
abstract: Abstract The task of predicting the influence of scientific research and ranking authors is a substantial difficulty that has attracted the attention of scientists in different fields of study. This task is crucial for improving research efficiency, supporting decision-making, and enabling scientific evaluations. Various indexes have been proposed by the scientific community to identify significant authors, including citation count, publication count, hybrid techniques, the h-index, and its variants. However, the scientific community does not agree on the most suitable single index for author ranking. This study presents a new index derived from a dataset in the field of Civil Engineering. The dataset consists of information from 500 authors, with an equal distribution between those who have not received awards and those who have received awards from prestigious civil engineering scientific societies during year 2011 to 2019. Initially, we ranked indices based on their values for each individual author to find the top parameters regularly placing awardees in the top 10% and 20% records. We also utilized Random Forest techniques to identify the top influential parameters. Subsequently, the correlation between the h-index and its various derivatives was calculated. A strong correlation suggested that these indices had a similar effect, while a weak correlation implied little or no relationship between them. The study leads us to suggest a new index derived by aggregating the top two parameters, so that it outperforms by 10% in terms of accuracy relative to the indices evaluated in this study. The awardees honored by different civil engineering societies serve as a benchmark for evaluating the impact of authors in this study. The awardees occurring in each index’s ranked list are determined, and the extent to which each index contributed to bringing awardees to the top is evaluated. It has been shown that the PI index is capable of placing up to accuracy 60% and 69% awardees positioned in the top 10% and 20% of ranked list respectively.

title: Decolonising Citation: Epistemic Injustice, Metrics, and Building Infrastructures for African Scholarship
authors: Eutychus Ngotho Gichuru; Archangel Byaruhanga Rukooko
institutions: Makerere University
abstract: The paper investigates how global citation systems and academic assessment methods continue to sustain colonial legacies. This study uses a decolonial theoretical framework which includes the concept of epistemic injustice to study how citation metrics create knowledge distribution imbalances. Our criticism originates from our position as African scholars who study Western academic journals and Western theoretical frameworks to fight against the Western systems which we aim to destroy. Our analysis process is guided by reflexive awareness. The bibliometric analysis of Scopus publication data between 2019 and 2023 shows how African journals and scholarship face marginalisation through their lower citation rates and the overwhelming dominance of English-language publications. The paper shows that current academic practices commit testimonial and hermeneutical injustice against African knowers. The solution we propose requires an approach to citation which accepts all knowledge forms that exist in oral and communal traditions and different languages. We argue that rather than avoiding the poison of existing colonial academic structures, scholars can strategically work within these systems to build immunity and create alternative infrastructures.

title: How aggregation shapes impact: a multidimensional evaluation framework for health-related academic spin-offs
institutions: KU Leuven; Flanders Make (Belgium); Eindhoven University of Technology
abstract: Abstract Evaluating the impact of academic spin-offs remains methodologically fragmented, with existing approaches relying on narrow indicators and rarely making their aggregation choices explicit or testable. This paper addresses both gaps by introducing a multidimensional impact framework with three distinctive contributions to academic entrepreneurship evaluation: it integrates five complementary impact dimensions–financial performance, organizational strength, innovation capacity, market impact, and societal impact–into a single coherent evaluation design; it incorporates an age-sensitive data strategy that adjusts for venture lifecycle stage, enabling meaningful comparison across spin-offs at different levels of maturity; and it operationalizes and empirically tests how alternative aggregation strategies shape composite evaluation outcomes–a methodological concern well-established in composite indicator design broadly, but not previously applied or tested at the venture level in academic entrepreneurship evaluation. The framework is applied to fifty-eight health-related spin-offs from KU Leuven, classified into Biotech, Medtech, and Digital Health clusters. Results reveal substantial heterogeneity in multidimensional impact profiles across clusters, and demonstrate that aggregation logic–not just indicator selection–fundamentally determines how impact is measured and ranked. Market-amplified aggregation produces greater score differentiation, particularly among Digital Health ventures, with direct implications for how universities and funding agencies interpret portfolio-level impact assessments. The result is a framework that is practically replicable–offering a template for universities, funding agencies, and policymakers seeking to move beyond narrow performance proxies, with the caveat that transferability to institutions with different portfolio compositions, TTO governance models, or data availability requires empirical validation in those contexts.

title: The scientific game
authors: Lutz Bornmann; Antonio Miguel  M. Osório
institutions: Max Planck Society; Universitat Rovira i Virgili
abstract: Using game theory, we demonstrate how performance metrics in academic science function as a non-monetary currency that solves the principal-agent problem in science and extracts high efforts from researchers. In light of increasingly scarce resources, these incentives require structural redesign of their mechanism to prevent strategic manipulation.

title: Journal-tiering systems as institutional devices in research evaluation: CAS, JCR, and rule-based governance in Chinese universities
authors: Yue Song; Zhongshuai Li; Yuan Gao
institutions: Changchun Institute of Technology; Jilin University
abstract: Abstract Journal-tiering systems can serve at least three distinct purposes: providing information about publication channels, offering formative guidance on where to publish, and supplying summative rules for evaluating completed research. This article examines how two influential citation-based systems, the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS) tiers and Journal Citation Reports (JCR) quartiles, are embedded in formal university policy texts in China and what evaluative functions they perform once institutionalised. Drawing on document- and clause-level content analysis of 29 publicly traceable policy documents, the study shows that JCR quartiles are used most visibly in procedural threshold rules, whereas CAS tiers appear more often in reward conversion, performance scoring, workload allocation, and some degree-related standards. Parallel CAS–JCR arrangements are concentrated in graded recognition frameworks. A second reading of non-quartile documents shows that removing explicit quartiles does not necessarily produce qualitative article-level assessment: journal-level governance may persist through internal catalogues and core-journal categories whose construction is not always disclosed. In the context of the discontinuation of CAS updates, the evidence supports a diagnosis of structural exposure rather than a claim of completed migration to JCR or another list. The article contributes a functional framework for distinguishing informational, formative, and determinative uses of journal-tiering systems and argues that reform should address the institutional consequences attached to journal categories, not merely substitute one classificatory carrier for another.

title: Metadatos bibliográficos abiertos para la cartografía institucional de bajo costo: Un ejercicio descriptivo en una Universidad Latinoamericana
institutions: Universidad Especializada de las Américas
abstract: Open scholarly infrastructures may offer resource-constrained Latin American universities a practical route for mapping research activity without relying exclusively on licensed databases. This study reports an exploratory methodological exercise that tested whether OpenAlex metadata could support a transparent, low-cost, and reproducible institutional baseline. A public university served as the demonstration case and was not treated as an object of performance assessment. The exercise produced a curated subcorpus of 221 high-confidence records with explicit affiliation evidence and classification in either the Social Sciences or Health Sciences domain. Frequencies and percentages were calculated by year, domain, primary field, document type, language, and number of authors. The resulting profile contained 170 records (76.9%) dated 2019-2025, 190 articles (86.0%), 177 Spanish-language records (80.1%), and 96 records (43.4%) with two or more authors. The exercise was informative because it converted dispersed public metadata into an internally consistent descriptive baseline while making its assumptions visible. The counts are research estimates rather than official institutional statistics and should not be interpreted as a ranking, audit, or evaluation of quality, impact, academic units, or individual performance.

title: Measured success and unspoken loss in China’s STEAM doctoral education
institutions: Zhejiang University
abstract: STEAM doctoral education promises to connect technical expertise with humanistic reflection, yet this aim becomes fragile when training is organised around measurable outputs. Drawing on 34 semi-structured interviews across seven research-intensive Chinese universities, the study examines how evaluation metrics shape the roles available to arts, humanities and social science perspectives within STEM-related doctoral work. Biesta’s concepts of qualification, socialisation and subjectification provide the primary framework, supported by Foucault’s account of governmentality. Three themes emerged: recalibrated metrics, instrumental interdisciplinarity and unspoken loss. Evaluation reform redefined measurable success without substantially reducing pressure, while humanistic perspectives gained legitimacy mainly when serving design, ethics, communication or public value. Candidates consequently reported less time and authority for critical questioning, ethical hesitation and non-instrumental inquiry. Metrics therefore operate pedagogically by shaping which questions count as doctoral progress, enabling interdisciplinary inclusion without necessarily granting humanistic inquiry epistemic authority.

title: Applications of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) Algorithms for Predicting Scholarly and Citation Impact
institutions: Lovely Professional University
venue: Advances in computational intelligence and robotics book series
abstract: Scholarly impact, a critical measure of the influence, significance, and contribution of academic endeavors, has traditionally been assessed using rudimentary metrics such as citation counts and peer reviews. While these conventional methods have served as benchmarks, they often fail to encapsulate the intricate and evolving nature of academic influence. Recent breakthroughs in artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) have significantly transformed this domain, enabling the development of more comprehensive, precise, and timely frameworks for assessing scholarly impact. This paper delves into the multifaceted applications of AI and ML in the realm of scholarly evaluation, with a particular focus on citation analysis, alternative metrics (altmetrics), and predictive analytics. Additionally, the paper examines the inherent challenges, ethical considerations, and future directions associated with harnessing these cutting-edge technologies to redefine academic assessment paradigms.

title: Research waste before research begins: the problem of research-priority mismatch in low- and middle-income countries
subfield: Public Health, Environmental and Occupational Health
abstract: Scholarship on research waste has concentrated on what goes wrong after a question has been chosen: flawed design, selective reporting, publication bias, and the slow attrition of findings that never reach the people who could use them. A more upstream loss has drawn far less scrutiny - the commitment of scarce resources to questions poorly matched to the needs of the populations expected to benefit from them. In this viewpoint, I argue that such research-priority mismatch is itself a distinct form of waste, and that its costs fall most heavily on low- and middle-income countries, where research budgets are thin and the opportunity cost of every funded project is correspondingly steep. Drawing on work in meta-research, scientometrics, responsible research assessment, and science policy, I examine how academic incentives can favour internationally visible topics over locally consequential ones, and how publication-based promotion, journal prestige, and bibliometric indicators can quietly entrench that preference. To name priority mismatch as waste is not to reject international collaboration or curiosity-driven inquiry; it is to ask for proportion between global participation and local relevance. I close with a review of ongoing reforms in funding, evaluation, and academic reward that might draw research investment back toward public benefit.

title: Publisher coverage bias in the Stanford/Ioannidis “top 2% of scientists” rankings
authors: Carl P. Lipo; Robert J. DiNapoli; Benjamin Andrus
institutions: Binghamton University
abstract: Abstract The “top 2% of scientists” rankings have grown in popularity as a means of research evaluation, with the potential to influence hiring, promotion, and funding decisions for over 230,000 researchers worldwide. We documented 123 universities across 32 countries and cited these rankings in official communications. The rankings rely exclusively on Scopus, a citation database owned by Elsevier, which also publishes a large portfolio of journals indexed in Scopus. We drew a stratified random sample of 600 researchers from the rankings (n=564 successfully matched) across book-heavy, mixed, and journal-heavy fields, and compared each researcher’s Scopus publication count to their OpenAlex record. Median Scopus coverage was 45.3% of OpenAlex publications. We documented systematic coverage disparities: researchers publishing in Elsevier journals had 30.6 percentage points higher coverage than those publishing elsewhere (20.8 pp under an any-Elsevier-vs-none contrast), even though our sample contained more than twice as many Oxford, Cambridge, Wiley, and Springer publications as Elsevier publications. The Elsevier coverage advantage persists even when comparing journals of similar citation impact. Book-focused scholars fare worse: humanities researchers show 43.6 percentage points lower coverage than STEM researchers, with Nobel and Pulitzer Prize winners among those affected. When we recalculated the rankings using the complete OpenAlex dataset, individual researchers shifted by a median of 142,276 positions, with the largest shift exceeding 1.2 million positions. These findings indicate that widely used scientist rankings may reflect both database coverage patterns and research impact, raising concerns about their use in career-determining decisions.

title: From policy transfer to policy plurality: pluriversal approaches to education policy-making
institutions: Dokuz Eylül University
abstract: Education systems often import ‘best practices’ on the assumption that models can travel intact across contexts. Drawing on policy translation, pluriversal thought, and epistemic justice, this conceptual article advances policy plurality as an alternative to policy replication. It argues that policy travel is an epistemic, ontological, and political problem concerning whose knowledge counts and how learning, evidence, achievement, and accountability are defined across unequal contexts. Through a critical conceptual synthesis, the article proposes a seven-component framework– context mapping, evidence plurality, co-design, multi-sited pilots with reverse transfer, a local lexicon, equivalence-based assessment, and an open learning loop– to support negotiated policy design. Three mini-cases on English-medium instruction, single-score assessment regimes, and micro-credentials illustrate how traveling reforms may be recontextualized through local meanings, plural evidence, and opportunity-to-learn indicators. As a pre-implementation contribution, the article reframes validity in terms of equivalence, treats contestation as central to policymaking, and offers a design-oriented framework for future empirical validation.

title: Health Communication: A Bibliometric Analysis
authors: Abdulkadir Güner; Emine Murt; Yılmaz DAŞLI
institutions: Sivas Cumhuriyet Üniversitesi
abstract: The purpose of this research is to examine the scientific trends, developmental trajectory, and structural characteristics of academic studies produced in the field of health communication using bibliometric methods. In this context, 9,518 studies published between 1972 and 2024 in the Web of Science (WoS) database and containing the terms "health communication" or "health and communication" in their titles were analyzed. R-based Biblioshiny for Bibliometrix software was used for data evaluation. The findings indicate that the first publication in the field was produced in 1972, that the studies were published in 2,316 different sources, that the annual publication growth rate was 14.52%, and that the average number of citations per document was 18.16. A consistent increase in the number of publications has been observed particularly after 2004, with a notable acceleration in 2019. The most productive journals are Health Communication, Journal of Health Communication, Patient Education and Counseling, and Journal of Medical Internet Research; while the most productive authors are Gary L. Kreps, Seth M. Noar, and Triveni Kuchi. The results reveal the development of health communication research and provide a guiding framework for future studies.

title: Discipline-Level Benchmarking of University Innovation Contributions in a Cross-Border Regional Innovation System: Evidence from the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area
authors: Naubahar Sharif; Ming De Pearl Ngau
institutions: Education University of Hong Kong; Hong Kong University of Science and Technology

title: Narratives of transparency: how do commercial and non-commercial providers of research information legitimize the datafication of research?
institutions: German Centre for Higher Education Research and Science Studies; Freie Universität Berlin; Weizenbaum Institute
abstract: The datafication of research has immensely expanded the possibilities for creating more metadata regarding research practice and performance. This has supported the growth of research information produced by commercial and non-commercial providers based on digital infrastructures including bibliometric databases, research information systems, and analytics services for the scientific community and beyond. In this paper, we ask how the providers of research information legitimize the need for the datafication of research and thus for their tools by looking at the providers’ narratives of transparency and how they differ according to their business model. Based on 22 expert interviews with employees of commercial and non-commercial organizations, we show that there are three narratives – demonstrating research performance, improving research, and supporting research governance – that build on distinct meanings of transparency, implying particular understandings of research practice and performance, which influence how research is made accessible and assessable through the metadata and analytics services the organizations provide.

title: Metrics of misrecognition
institutions: Makerere University
venue: International Journal of Ethics and Systems
abstract: Purpose This conceptual paper aims to provide a critical analysis of the practice arrangement bundles governing promotion and evaluation systems within flagship universities as a socioeconomic system profoundly shaping academic identity and institutional ethics. Design/methodology/approach Using an empirical Ricoeurian hermeneutic operationalized into five steps – (1) purposive selection of scholarly texts from the higher education literature covering promotion and evaluating and governing systems, (2) a hermeneutic of suspicion in systematically questioning the text-based ideology of each of the documents, (3) a hermeneutic of recovery to highlight the possibility of alternative meanings and ethical perspectives, (4) an integration of disparate interpretations into four interpretive provocations, (5) to maintain an audit trail to safeguard the intelligibility of interpretation, this research presents its workings by detailing an applied instance of application of the hermeneutical circle. Findings The analysis reveals that the promotion system functions as a practice arrangement bundle that perpetuates a metricized ethical economy characterized by misrecognition, asymmetry and instability. This system forces academics into identity negotiation fraught with epistemic violence and moral injury, displacing institutional responsibility onto individuals while systematically devaluing care, collegiality and slow scholarship. Originality/value Firstly, the methodological contribution of the author’s paper is that the author provides a replicable approach to using the hermeneutical circle (from Ricœur’s philosophical hermeneutics) in institutional analysis. Secondly, the author’s conceptual contribution is that the author enrich the conceptual lenses of institutional misrecognition (from Sennett) and narrative foreclosure (from Bruner) with our empirical findings on academia promotion practices.

title: The impact of changing metrics in Shanghai Ranking’s Global Ranking of Academic Subjects on medical sciences subjects
institutions: Széchenyi István University; Ludovika University of Public Service
abstract: Abstract This article examines the longitudinal stability, internal consistency, and stratifying effects of Shanghai Ranking’s Global Ranking of Academic Subjects (Shanghai GRAS) in six subjects of Medical Sciences (2017–2025). While Shanghai GRAS has gained prominence as a global higher education benchmark, little is known about the empirical consequences of its methodological changes. Using a quantitative approach combining descriptive statistics, indicator score and overall score change analysis, and K-means clustering, we evaluated the effects of indicator revisions, weight adjustments, and new data sources on institutional trajectories. Our findings show that global methodological alterations influencing all subjects generate substantial volatility, especially for institutions outside the top clusters. The 2019 Category Normalized Citation Impact revision corresponded with overall score increases, while the 2024 methodology restructuring led to significant score declines in general, but the rankings of leading institutions either improved or were not affected. Our findings challenge assumptions about the comparability of rankings and reveal their performative role in reinforcing institutional hierarchies, while also calling for more transparent, context-sensitive evaluation frameworks that reflect the epistemic diversity of global academia.

title: What makes some research papers more 'popular' than others? Inferential network analysis insights into technology leadership research in the field of educational administration
institutions: Wenzhou University; Wenzhou-Kean University
abstract: Decades of bibliometric research have illuminated intellectual development and knowledge production in educational administration, yet less is known about the citation motivations underlying scholarly communication. This study investigates citation behaviours in technology leadership research, using a fine-grained network analysis approach. Results reveal three tensions shaping citation patterns: established versus emerging scholars, journal prestige versus journal coverage, and homophily versus diversification. Established scholars exert a consolidating influence on citation networks, while emerging scholars increasingly cite one another. Journal inbreeding, gender, ethnicity, and national affiliations shape citation decisions. These findings extend bibliometric research by showing how citation practices reflect broader patterns of academic recognition and social affiliation. They also have implications for citation equity, doctoral training, editorial policy, and research evaluation. Universities, publishers, and funding agencies can use such insights to support more transparent and inclusive scholarly communication, creating greater space for both established and emerging scholars to contribute to the field.

title: Research quality metrics as a complement to bibliometrics: an opinion paper
authors: Harald Hannerz; Kristian Schultz Hansen; Jan Hyld Pejtersen; Helene Kless Willadsen
institutions: National Research Centre for the Working Environment; VIVE - The Danish Center for Social Science Research
abstract: Abstract Substantial proportions of research investment may be wasted due to flawed study design, biased reporting, and publication bias, raising concerns about how research performance is evaluated. Despite this, current assessment systems rely heavily on bibliometric indicators such as publication counts, co-authorship, and citation metrics, which do not reliably reflect research quality or scientific rigor. In this opinion paper, we argue that such indicators may reward practices that undermine the accumulation of reliable knowledge, including p-hacking, selective reporting, and underpowered study designs, while undervaluing essential contributions such as replication research. We propose that bibliometric measures should be complemented by transparent and auditable research quality metrics, including indicators of reproducibility, statistical power, risk of bias, and adherence to reporting standards. We further suggest that recent advances in large language models may facilitate the scalable implementation of such metrics. Adopting quality-focused indicators could improve research evaluation and help reduce avoidable research waste.

title: Challenges, discomfort, resistance, and strategic ways forward: addressing researcher resistance to EDI principles in Canadian NSE research
institutions: Toronto Metropolitan University; Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada
abstract: Equity, diversity, and inclusion (EDI) are increasingly recognized as foundational to research excellence, yet many researchers in the natural sciences and engineering (NSE) remain uncertain about, or resistant to, integrating EDI principles into their work. In this Perspectives article, we examine how discomfort, confusion, and active resistance to EDI arise within Canadian NSE research cultures shaped by historically narrow notions of merit, objectivity, and excellence. Drawing on scholarship in research culture, behaviour, and organizational change, as well as literature on ethics and bias, we analyze common forms of resistance, from passive apathy and performative compliance to overt backlash, anti-“woke” rhetoric, and zero-sum thinking. We then outline practical, evidence-informed strategies for researchers, teams, institutions, and funders to recognize, interpret, and respond to these dynamics in ways that reduce friction, protect those advancing EDI, and keep momentum toward culture change. As a companion to Webb and Coe (submitted), which focuses on funder-level interventions, this paper centres the everyday practices and decision points where EDI, ethics, and excellence intersect in NSE research.
